item.title: Seeing Like John Berger - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The writer and critic John Berger — that “anarchist-angel,” as essayist Megan O’Grady calls him in a review of his new biography — very much shaped the way we see. Berger himself had asked the novelist Tom Overton to wait until his death to write his biography; arriving nearly a decade after, the result is perceptive, illuminating, and an aesthetic work in its own right. 

It’s good reading when paired with Channelle Chevelle Russell’s review of an exhibition of Deana Lawson’s photographs at Gagosian Gallery in Manhattan. Lawson turns her camera’s gaze to beauty-supply surveillance photos of customers, which are often pinned behind the counter to deter theft. The gallery does not allow visitors to take photographs of the exhibition. 

The resulting questions are deeply Bergerian, if I may: Who gets to look? Who gets looked at? Who has the power to determine what an image means?

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

John Berger in His Own Bruised Time

These days, we tend to take his ideas for granted: that art — making it or contemplating it — creates knowledge. That by foregrounding the processes by which we see, we can discover the mechanisms and deceptions through which we make meaning. And, of course, that it’s important to know who is footing the bill. John Berger, who died in 2017, was famous not for challenging the Western canon but for making its revelations feel so evidently connected to everything else about life. His essays often read like personal letters, offering to us the gift of our own passions and imaginations. | Megan O’Grady

I totally agree. I knew Roy briefly in the early 90s, when I was working with Gemini G.E.L. I was in charge of drawing his stripes at a perfect 70-degree angle on the woodcuts for his Bedroom print. I was 22, he was 77, so I was flattered when he asked me to dinner because I thought a young artist could learn from one of the most famous pop artists of that century. All he said about his art was that he needed to hold back some prints so he didn't flood the market and drive prices down. The rest of the meal was an uncomfortable experience so many of us have discussed in the #metoo movement. I never discovered anything deeper about his work, and my personal experience tainted my impression of him as an artist and a man.

item.title: Collector’s Diary: Chang Osathanugrah Reflects on What It Means to See Art with Fresh Eyes After Years of Looking - ARTnews.com
item.description:
I hadn’t expected a talking frog to remind me of why I fell in love with contemporary art, and I certainly hadn’t expected to lose it before I ever had the chance to buy it.

In March, during a stretch of cool weather that reminds me why I still love Hong Kong, even when it no longer feels quite like the place I remember, I came across Ryan Gander’s 2025 sculpture You Complete Me, or I see things you can’t see (A Frog’s Tale) at Esther Schipper’s booth at Art Basel Hong Kong. In the surreal work, a hyperreal frog perched in a potted plant speaks in the voice of a young girl, whose dialogue moves through a stream of existential musing, both innocent and eerily profound. It was like entering a fairy tale that understood something true about being human. The gallerist delivered the news with the gentleness reserved for a hopeful collector: the work was not available. Someone else, it turned out, had already claimed the frog. I have long made peace with losing works to other collectors, but losing this one cut deeper than past ones had.

What the piece did, before I learned I couldn’t have it, was interrupt a fatigue I had begun to accept as ordinary, and one I doubt is mine alone. Call it art fair fatigue, or something closer to a low-key art world malaise; either diagnosis feels apt, and I suspect half the convention center that week was nursing the same undiagnosed condition. For a few minutes, I was not thinking about price, provenance, market cycles, or where a work sat within the artist’s practice. I was not evaluating anything at all. I was simply looking, the way I did as a child. That giddy feeling has stayed with me since.

As a small consolation, Gander is already in the collection of Dib Bangkok, the private museum that was my father’s lifelong dream and that we opened at the end of 2025, two years after his death. Ahead of the museum’s inauguration, we acquired Gander’s Untouched Idea Machines (2025), a wall-mounted brass dispenser that prints out one of some 2,000 unrealized ideas for artworks at the press of a button. We plan to put it on view in our second show this fall. Under the circumstances, it seemed only fitting to go home with an idea rather than a frog.

This was also one of the least traveled years I have had in some time: business responsibilities, it turns out, have their own gravity, and this year has kept me literally grounded in Bangkok, with only brief trips to Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Singapore, including a panel at Art SG on the responsibilities of building museums today.

A Shanghai trip came in late April, ostensibly for a Monocle talk to a room of entrepreneurs, though the real draw was at a viewing room on Taicang Road, in the old French Concession, where a series of Paul Chan works were being considered for Dib’s collection, including 2nd Light (2006). A part of Chan’s “Seven Lights” series, this now 20-year-old installation features shadows of trees, flags, and falling figures drifting across the floor in light alone, the room taking on the quality of a dream where beauty and fragility coexist. Light, I realized, can be as expressive as pigment or bronze, and this work asked only that I dwell a little longer in the uncertainty than felt comfortable, which is perhaps closer to what experiencing art should be.

Still, I keep returning to one question, and a guiding one for Dib: Where does depth meet accessibility? Can a deeply considered work remain intellectually rewarding while still speaking to someone encountering it for the very first time? I do not believe those two worlds are as far apart as we tend to assume.

Watching thousands of first-time visitors move through Dib this year has only confirmed it. Experienced collectors don’t necessarily see more than beginners; we simply know more, and that is not the same thing. Children rarely ask what movement a work belongs to. They ask why it feels alive, or why it seems strange. Expertise can overwhelm wonder if we allow it to. The challenge is not learning more about art. It is remembering how to look at it. That really has been the personal question for me these past months: How does one keep seeing art with fresh eyes after so many years of looking at it?

Sadly, I had to forego the Venice Biennale this year; business kept me in Bangkok. But our director Miwako Tezuka went on Dib’s behalf and came back talking about Lorna Simpson’s exhibition, “Third Person” at Punta della Dogana, one of two Venice exhibition spaces of fellow Top 200 Collector François Pinault. What struck Miwako most was Stacked Stones/Vibrating Cycles (2020), an installation of stacked stones crowned with singing bowls that visitors are invited to sound themselves. The tones rising off it, she said, echoed the late artist Montien Boonma’s view of art as practice rather than spectacle, gently urging humility over hubris. Hearing about that piece, my FOMO was very real.

Miwako said she took something else away from the bowls when she sounded them herself, something close to home. She said it was the closest thing she’d experienced all year to something our first show had been reaching for. “(In)visible Presence” was built around memory: my late father, my grandfather, Boonma’s work, and the core community of people who made Dib possible long before the institution existed. It was a somber show that never asked anyone to look away from loss but tried instead to embody what it means to experience loss. In essence, it was an ode to spiritual reconciliation.

“Giving Life,” our second exhibition, will mark the moment we finally allow ourselves to celebrate again. Featuring around 30 artists, including Alexander Calder, Rirkrit Tiravanija, and Izumi Kato, the show explores the many ways artists breathe new life into materials, objects, and ideas. What fascinates me most is how some begin with things that already carry their own histories: spent bomb shells, living plants, old machinery. Objects shaped by conflict, time, or everyday use are transformed into something unexpectedly alive. Many of these works were made while their countries were at war, their economies were collapsing, or authoritarian governments were tightening their grip on the freedoms that make life feel like your own person. Yet together they make a quiet but unmistakable case for life itself. That feels worth celebrating. Perhaps this abundance of life is my own response to the undiagnosed malaise I carried home from art fairs. Whatever it is, it already seems to be working.

Away from museums, the market has continued its own reckoning over the past year. The top of the auction world and the prices for historical artists kept climbing while blue-chip, middle-market names looked shakier: a natural cycle, it seems to me. In other news, and to my joy, René Magritte deservedly became one of the market’s most sought-after names, proof that quality paired with scarcity only boosts appetite. This past June, Sotheby’s London sold La Belle Promenade (1965) for $21.6 million, while the house’s Paris branch sold La Magie Noire (1934) for $12.3 million in October 2025.

The subtle painterly quality that draws me to Magritte also brings me much closer to home, to the paintings of Prae Pupityastaporn, whose work I have collected for almost a decade. A visit in early June to Sutima Sucharitakul’s Nova Contemporary in Bangkok’s Samyan-Rama4 area deepened my appreciation of her work. Pupityastaporn takes ordinary subjects—a window or a landscape, for example—and suspends them in a real yet eerie, quietly humming dreamscape, softer and more interior than Magritte’s. There is a silent magic within the mundanity in her work that reminds me that within our everyday lives there is actually something quite sublime. It’s this quality that makes her one of Thailand’s most exciting and unique painters.

Right now, there is a generational story unfurling. The children of collectors (myself excluded, having apparently missed the rebellious gene) do not always wish to inherit their parents’ taste, and I understand the instinct, even if I never quite felt it myself. Someone actually complained to me not long ago that their parents had bought a Monet. I digress. Yes, it’s hard to watch, though I suspect what’s really at stake has less to do with taste than with the relationship between parent and child, playing itself out through whatever does or doesn’t end up on the walls at home.

Nonetheless, I’ve been feeling unusually optimistic about Thailand this year. It seems to me that a newer style of gallery, built more around community and vibe, is answering that gap. It feels like its own coming-of-age story is still being written. Bangkok Kunsthalle, for example, continues to push forward in Yaowarat; the Jim Thompson Art Center is still building on the momentum Gridthiya (Jeab) Gaweewong created there; and Central Group’s deCentral, led by my old schoolmate Punn Chirakiti, opens next year. Moreover, there seems to be a growing wave of new collectors and patrons entering Bangkok’s cultural scene. Together, they’ve kept me far more entertained close to home than any frog in the bustle of an art fair ever managed. None of it is mine to take credit for, which is perhaps why it has been such a pleasure simply to watch it unfold.

Being grounded at home, as it turned out, wasn’t so bad. It gave me an excuse to sit still and reflect. Collecting has taught me a great deal over the years. Going back to Gander’s frog, I’m reminded that art is not something we are necessarily meant to fully understand. The works that remain with us are rarely the ones we can completely explain. They are the ones that change how we see the world and, every so often, remind us how to see it at all.

item.title: Christie’s London Sales Bring in $289 M., With Records for Bridget Riley and Liubov Popova - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Christie’s London brought in £218.6 million ($289.4 million) across two evening sales Wednesday, more than doubling last year’s total and offering an encouraging sign for the art market ahead of the New York auctions next month.

Seven auction records were set, including five during the sale of British businessman Peter Simon’s collection, while a Wassily Kandinsky painting fetched £31.6 million ($41.8 million) in the evening’s second auction. (All prices reported include buyer’s premium.)

The two sales, which coincide with Frieze London and Frieze Masters, achieved a combined sell-through rate of 91 percent by lot and 96 percent by value. The Simon collection, which several market insiders described to ARTnews as the real attraction in London this week, accounted for £107.5 million ($142.3 million) of the total, making it the highest-value single-owner collection ever sold at Christie’s London. The subsequent 20th- and 21st-century sale brought in £111.1 million ($147 million).

There was, however, some confusion about when the festivities were supposed to begin. Although the Simon sale started at 6 p.m., in some places Christie’s live-auction website advertised a 7 p.m. start time. At least three market professionals, including an adviser with a global clientele, had understood that the sale would begin at the later hour. Whether the hiccup caused anyone to miss bidding remains unclear.

Even still, Christie’s was packed when the “Monsoon: The Peter Simon Collection” sale began. Assembled by the founder British retailer Monsoon who has appeared on each edition of ARTnews’s Top 200 Collectors list since 2005, the collection sold 98 percent by lot and 99 percent by value, with only one of the 41 works failing to find a buyer.

One of the evening’s biggest surprises came from Russian avant-garde painter Liubov Popova, whose Painterly Architectonic sold for £7.64 million ($10.1 million), more than three times its £2.5 million ($3.3 million) high estimate. Setting a new auction record for the artist, the work saw nearly eight minutes of bidding both in the room and on the phones.

Other records set Wednesday came for Bridget Riley’s Streak 2, which £5.21 million ($6.9 million), and David Bomberg’s San Miguel, Toledo, Afternoon, which brought £3.26 million ($4.32 million). The bidding for the Bomberg work had the room cheering, and the auctioneer even asked for a closer inspection of the painting. Further records were achieved for Portia Zvavahera and Barbara Hepworth.

The Simon collection’s most expensive work, Francis Bacon’s Figure in Movement, fetched £17.19 million ($22.8 million), selling to a bidder in the room, while Piet Mondrian’s Composition A, with Double Line and Yellow brought £9.71 million ($12.86 million). Joan Miró’s Peinture (Les amants – Adam et Eve) sold for £8.56 million ($11.33 million), and Hurvin Anderson’s Last House brought £5.7 million ($7.5 million) against an estimate of £2 million–£3 million ($2.6 million–$3.9 million).

Philip Hoffman, chairman and founder of the Fine Art Group, told ARTnews before the sale that a handful of works in Simon’s collection would race ahead while much of the rest would sell with relatively little competition. Buyers at Frieze Masters, he said, had been holding back money in anticipation of the auction.

Afterward, Hoffman called the two sales a clear indication of a solid market, though he cautioned against reading too much into the totals, especially since 29 of the 41 lots in the Simon evening sale carried third-party guarantees, meaning much of the financial risk had already been accounted for before bidding began.

“These auctions are staged, managed, and already pumped up to the max for the best guarantees they can get,” he told ARTnews.

By the time the auction’s final two paintings, Glenn Ligon’s Large Silver In Show Business and Beatriz Milhazes’s O Rapaz (The Boy), each sold for £192,000 ($250,000) against low estimates of £400,000 ($529,000) and £300,000 ($397,000), respectively, the room was mute.

In the short break before the 20th/21st Century evening sale, the energy returned, with two Josef Albers works exceeding their estimates, followed by René Magritte’s Le seize septembre, fetching £3.26 million ($4.3 million), well above its £1.8 million ($2.4 million) high estimate.

The zing of the Brits could be felt when David Hockney’s Dog Painting 17 came under the hammer. The painting, appearing at auction for the first time, prompted applause and a spirited contest involving Christie’s London specialist Edmond Francey and at least three other specialists bidding by telephone. It eventually fetched £3.51 million ($4.64 million).

The patriotic spirit continued with British painter Flora Yukhnovich’s Capriccio, which fetched £2.2 million ($2.9 million), against a high estimate of £1.5 million ($1.98 million).

But silence fell over the room for Mondrian’s Composition III (1920), as spectators and bidders alike took out their cameras to record the moment the painting sold for £25.2 million ($33.4 million), squarely in the middle of its £20 million–£30 million ($26.5 million–$39.7 million) estimate.

Though the Mondrian was expected to achieve the highest price going into the auction, Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben proved to be the bigger attraction. Auctioneer Adrien Meyer described it as “the most important early work by the artist to ever come to auction.” Nearly 20 bids ricocheted across the room, with Christie’s specialists Amelia Walker, Katharine Arnold, and Maria Los competing for the work. Los ultimately secured the painting on a £27 million ($35.7 million) hammer bid, bringing the final price to £31.56 million ($41.79 million), against a £25 million high estimate. The painting had been restituted to the heirs of Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann in 2023.

As with the first sale, the mood changed again toward the end of the auction. At the 27th lot, Warhol’s Mona Lisa (Reversal Series), which ultimately sold for £1.5 million ($1.98 million), Meyer stepped away from the rostrum and Yu Ge Wang took over. What followed was a difficult stretch, with works by Cy Twombly, George Condo, Alberto Giacometti, and Lucian Freud among those failing to find buyers. By 8:52 p.m., the sea of polished loafers and designer handbags had started to disappear.

Even a charitable cause could not entirely revive the room. Igshaan Adams’s The certainty of being a rose (ii), a sculpture made of beads, thread and textile, fetched £96,000 ($127,000) despite the auctioneer reminding bidders that proceeds would benefit environmental charities. The result nevertheless established an auction record for the artist.

The second sale finished with an 85 percent sell-through rate by lot, well below the Simon collection’s 98 percent. Yet with two works selling for more than £25 million, the combined results gave Christie’s plenty to celebrate ahead of its New York sales, which begin November 17.

For Hoffman, the evening’s results were encouraging but not necessarily conclusive, and the extensive use of guarantees should be taken with a grain of salt. He added that he waiting for the sale of the Antonio Homem Sonnabend collection, estimated to bring more than $50 million and offered without guarantees, for a clearer reading of the market.

item.title: As Diplomatic Tensions Persist, British Museum Chairman ‘Optimistic’ on Parthenon Marbles Deal - ARTnews.com
item.description:
George Osborne, chairman of the British Museum, has expressed hope that a deal can be struck to share the Parthenon Marbles between Athens and London, despite the two-centuries-long diplomatic feud.

“I’m still optimistic that we can reach an agreement,” Osborne told reporters in Athens on Tuesday. “If everyone enters into it with the spirit of we’re not going to get everything we want, as is always the case with a successful agreement, then there’s a deal to be done.”

The Parthenon Marbles, made between 447 and 432 BCE by the Greek sculptor Phidias, depict gods and processions in marble relief panels, sculptures, and friezes. They’re also known as the Elgin Marbles, after the Scottish nobleman Lord Elgin, who was the British ambassador to Constantinople. Elgin removed the sculptures from the Acropolis in Athens in 1801, while Greece was under Ottoman occupation. He later sold the sculptures to the British government, which has housed them in the British Museum ever since.

Greece has sought the marbles’ return since gaining independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1832, arguing that Elgin had no legal grounds to remove them. British officials, meanwhile, have cited the British Museum Act 1963, which prohibits the museum from deaccessioning objects in its collection, as justification for retaining the sculptures. Tensions between the two countries have escalated in recent years, fueled by the opening of a dedicated museum for the marbles in Athens and reports of leaks and other preservation concerns in the British Museum’s galleries.

“I very much hope we can come to some arrangement whereby the Parthenon sculptures that are in London can be seen in Athens but they have to be shared,” Osborne said Tuesday. “I know that’s not the position of everyone in Greece, and I understand that and respect that, but that is our position, and so if we want to make progress, it has to be in that spirit.”

Osborne’s comments follow a September op-ed by Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis published in the Guardian, in which he took issue with British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan’s characterization of France’s loan of the Bayeux Tapestry as “a very compelling example of international partnership.” Cullinan had suggested that a similar model of “reciprocal exchange” could be applied to the Parthenon Marbles.

“Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it,” he writes, “Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures.”

Osborne, a former Chancellor of the Exchequer, has been at the forefront of negotiations between the British Museum and Greece. In 2023, the London institution confirmed that it had been in talks with the Acropolis Museum, saying it was close to finalizing a deal under which the sculptures would return to Greece over time as part of a cultural exchange. The agreement never materialized. Greek Culture Minister Lina Mendoni told reporters days later that Greece would not accept a deal affirming the United Kingdom’s ownership claim. Instead, she proposed an exchange that would ensure treasures from Greek antiquity, including objects of comparable prestige to the Parthenon Marbles, would remain on display in London.

World leaders are set to convene at the EU-UK summit in Brussels next month. Speaking at a conference at the University of Athens on October 6, Mitsotakis suggested that discussions on diplomatic ties between the European Union and the United Kingdom, which voted to leave the bloc in 2016, would involve the British Museum dispute.

“The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate. This is not just an issue for Greece, it’s an issue for Europe,” Mitsotakis said.

item.title: Israel Returns 22 Looted Antiquities to Greece - ARTnews.com
item.description:
On Tuesday, the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) returned 22 antiquities to Greece. The cache includes decorated pottery from the 8th through the 4th centuries BCE that had been seized during an illegal antiquities trafficking investigation in and around Tel Aviv in 2020.

The ceremony took place at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens and was attended by Lina Mendoni, the Greek Minister of Culture; Pninat Yanai, the Israeli Ambassador to Greece; and Amir Ganor, director of the IAA’s Anti Theft Prevention Unit. This handover marks the first time Israel has returned contested items to Greece.

In a social media post, the IAA states that the 2020 seizure involved raids of an unnamed gallery, warehouses, and apartments which uncovered “thousands of archaeological items from Israel and around the world.” The investigation was prompted by suspicion of looting at ancient sites in the Mediterranean. The IAA does not clarify why it took Israel six years to return the items to Greece, or if objects belonging to other nations are also in the process of being repatriated. It is also not clear from where in Greece the items were looted.

Among the items back on Greek soil are black- and red-figure vessels, some with handles, decorated with scenes from Greek mythology, and would have been used in everyday life or as burial offerings. Among the vases of varying shapes and sizes (15 Attic vessels and six Corinthian, according to the Jerusalem Post) was a bronze female figure.

Lina Mendoni, the Greek Minister of Culture, said that “this return lays the foundation for deepening cooperation between our countries in the field of protecting cultural heritage. Every return of antiquities to their country of origin also carries with it a broad moral and symbolic significance.”

She added that the return, “reminds us all that protecting cultural heritage is a shared responsibility, and that the effective fight against the illegal trade in antiquities requires cooperation between countries, mutual trust, and a commitment to upholding the law and strengthening heritage.”

item.title: Why Pageant Is Suddenly All the Rage - Hyperallergic
item.description:
On a Friday morning in late August, dozens packed a small auditorium at the Museum of Modern Art to watch choreographer, director, and writer Isa Spector writhe on a red-painted platform, struggling to carry out the museum’s request to make “a painting of dance” in 10 minutes. After flailing to and fro, down on all fours to the red platform floor and up to the fluorescent studio lights, and calling out to a "mom" whose name changed to “MoMA” and a "dad" to “Dada” with an alliterative tongue, Spector had an epiphany. They knew what they were to paint. Seconds later, five performers donning red gloves emerged from backstage and assembled at the center of the platform. Hand in hand, they began twirling in a circle, staging a living parody of Matisse’s modernist masterpiece displayed in the galleries just a floor above.

The five subjects of this commissioned “painting” — Sharleen Chidiac, Lili Dekker, Jade Manns, Owen Prum, and Alexa West — are the co-founders of Pageant, an artist-run Brooklyn performance space that held a month-long residency at MoMA in August. "MoMAlogue #1" inaugurated Pageant’s seven-hour MoMA performance marathon, of which Spector’s was the first, but certainly not the only, meditation on dance’s relationship to its own history and that of visual art across 25 10-minute performances.

“I think the history of dance, coming from a ballet proscenium stage into modernism, then into postmodernism, started with a pictorial form,” artist and choreographer West said in a group interview with Hyperallergic after the Pageant Presents Pageant marathon. “And it’s slowly been breaking away from that over time.”

Preceded by a different space that Manns and Chidiac ran out of their apartment, Pageant was established in 2022 in a third-story loft on Graham Avenue in East Williamsburg. According to West, there was initially “no clear marketing vision” for Pageant. It was merely a solution to the group’s shared desire “to provide context to our practices in a post-COVID landscape in which there were very few opportunities to show work at our stage of artmaking.”

“We didn’t set out with the intention for it to be like an institution,” Chidiac added during the interview. “We just needed a space to work, to show our work, and to show other people’s work.

item.title: Monumental Statues of Ramses II Discovered in Egypt - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Archaeologists in Egypt have uncovered the remains of two colossal statues believed to depict Ramses II after a local landowner reported finding an inscribed stone block in the village of Behbeit El-Hagar.

The discoveries were made by an archaeological mission from Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA). According to Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, Secretary-General of the SCA, the first find was a stone head more than five-feet-high from a massive statue. It depicts a man wearing a double crown, a symbol of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt worn by ancient Egyptian rulers.

Nearby, archaeologists found part of the statue’s back pillar. An inscription on the pillar gives one of Ramses II’s five royal titles, “Hor-Ka-Nakht-Mery-Maat” (The Strong Bull, Beloved of Ma’at), identifying him as the sculpture’s subject.

The second find consists of part of a statue of a royal personage along with its head, which was adorned with the striped cloth associated with ancient Egyptian rulers. Not including the head, the surviving section of the figure, which is missing its legs and base, measures almost eight feet high. Based on the similarity of this statue’s face to that of the first, researchers believe it may also represent Ramses II, though the identification has not been confirmed.

The archaeological mission also found a pink granite block about four feet long not far from the statues. It bears traces of hieroglyphic inscriptions that include two more titles of Ramses II: “Nesu-Bity” (King of Upper and Lower Egypt) and “Sa-Ra” (Son of Ra).

Ramses II, known to historians as Ramses the Great, was the third king of ancient Egypt’s 19th Dynasty (1292–1191 BCE). He presided over the final peak of Egypt’s imperial power and is remembered for his 66-year rule, military campaigns, extensive building programs, and monumental temples and statues. Because of his popularity, longevity, and talent for political propaganda, inscriptions and artworks bearing his name and image can be found throughout Egypt.

Excavations and archaeological work are continuing in the area.

Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance, the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.

It’s fun to celebrity watch the entrance to Frieze London in Regent’s Park before the fair begins. As the floodgates opened for the VIP preview on Wednesday, Oscar-nominated actor Andrew Garfield and his girlfriend, actress Monica Barbaro, strolled in. Also present were Tilda Swinton, Bianca Jagger, London-based designer Dilara Findikoglu, and Raf Simons, Prada’s Belgium-based co-creative director and a longtime art collector. “I like everything about London,” Simons told ARTnews, “especially its people.”

The night before, amid the horde at the opening of Thaddaeus Ropac’s Georg Baselitz show, actor Damian Lewis was sizing up the big canvases. A couple of blocks down, you could find Serpentine Galleries artistic director Hans Ulrich Obrist casting his discerning eye at a Turner-inspired Rirkrit Tiravanija seascape at Pilar Corrias gallery. The starry showing for London’s offerings this week suggested that the city’s art scene still has life in it, even if some skipped it entirely for Paris, where Art Basel opens next week.

It’s not worth rehashing the well-worn—and, at this point, tedious—London-versus-Paris debate. But most people weren’t talking about it, either, on Wednesday at Frieze. Here’s some of what sold by the end of the fair’s first day. (While some of the mega-galleries post big ticket sales, it’s hard to gauge the overall health of the art market at art fairs because overall sales data is not made public. Plus, galleries self-report their sales, which makes them tough to verify.)

The mega-galleries have been relegated to the back of the fair’s tent, to give smaller players the spotlight near the fair’s entrance. Yet the placement did not deter Hauser & Wirth from selling most of its work by noon. Zoe Sperling, a partner at the gallery, told ARTnews she’d seen “a lot of American and Asian collectors.”

More than 20 pieces sold at Hauser & Wirth’s booths at Frieze London and Frieze Masters, totaling a sum of more than $11 million. Among the works sold were two Francis Picabia paintings, one untitled work from the 1940s sold for €1.1 million and Transparence, visage de femme (1928–29) for six-figures.

“There’s been tremendous energy here this morning,” Sperling said. “One of the things we’re really seeing is the interest from historic collectors that were maybe once more interested in traditional works and are now looking at contemporary works to complement their collections.” Avery Singer’s Solver (v.3), 2026, sold for $800,000, George Condo’s Figure Composition(2026) for $600,000, Lee Bul’s Perdu—Silhouette VII (2026) for $290,000, and Christina Kimeze’s Game on (crane’s cut), 2026, for $195,000.

The gallery also did well at Frieze Masters, where the offerings skew historical. Jan Brueghel the Elder’s Still Life of Flowers in a Stoneware Vase (1607–8) sold for around £5 million (about $6.58 million). “It’s one of the most important works we’ve ever been involved with,” Iwan Wirth, the gallery’s president and cofounder, told ARTnews. “The painting, made in the 17th century, stands as an exemplar of the kind of genius that contemporary artists look to in their own practice.”

At Lehmann Maupin’s Frieze London booth, more than 10 works sold, including McArthur Binion’s dna:sketch (2024) for $150,000. Other notable works included Liza Lou’s Azure (2015) for $140,000 and Alex Prager’s Ceremony (2026) for $60,000. The gallery also said it sold several works by UK-based artists to private collections, varying from three new paintings by Billy Childish in the range of £50,000–£60,000 ($65,900 to $79,100), to two new paintings by Freya Douglas-Morris in the range of £30,000–£50,000 ($39,000–$65,900), to two new works by Rana Begum in the range of £25,000 to £40,000 ($33,000–$52,600).

The British capital has a contagious energy, according to those who made a sale on the first day. “London is buzzing. It is helped by its proximity to Art Basel Paris, as many international collectors and museums are coming first to London and then go on to Paris. Two very different birds with one stone,” Sadie Coles, who runs her eponymous London gallery, told ARTnews. “There is depth here, and so much on offer for visitors from outstanding younger galleries to major exhibitions in museums.”

Perrotin’s solo booth of Izumi Kato’s paintings and sculptures sold for up to $250,000 each. The gallery had other notable sales from Oli Epp, whose new paintings sold for $55,000 each, and Shim Moon-Seup, who had a painting that fetched above $63,000. There was also a sculpture by Alma Allen, the artist controversially representing the United States at the Venice Biennale who will soon have a Perrotin show in Paris. It sold for $60,000.

David Zwirner moved 13 works that accounted for $4.55 million in sales. The top five pieces were paintings from Michaël Borremans for $1.5 million, a Dana Schutz for $900,000, a Lisa Yuskavage for $450,000, a Portia Zvavahera for $300,000, and a a Sasha Gordon for $400,000, the latter of which went to a European museum that the gallery did not identify. “Frieze London is still bringing people in, and it’s not just local collectors. It has been a good international morning,” James Green, associate partner and head of David Zwirner’s London gallery told ARTnews.

Rather than solely hanging its art on the wall, White Cube experimented with a metal frame for its booth featuring sketches by Ilana Savdie. The gallery recorded $1.55 million in sales, with Savdie’s painting The Great Compromise (2026) selling for $175,000 and Conspiracy of the Barons(2026) for $165,000. “The history of a place like this [London] is really hard to ignore,” Savdie told ARTnews. “I look to a lot of the artists that have been based here and the movements that have taken place, there are incredible museums to be inspired by. I haven’t spent enough time here to really be able to speak to it, but from afar I’m a big admirer.”

Edel Assanti’s sales included the placement of two paintings by Thornton Dial, with prices ranging $160,000 to $230,000.

Collectors at the fair came from near and far. Selim Bouafsoun, the Tunisian collector based in Dubai, told ARTnews he bought Tamo Jugeli’s Swan in Lake (2026) from Bukia Vakhania for $40,000 and Jonathan Okoronkwo’s Wilderness Be the Anthem Rydee (2026) from London’s Emalin gallery for €20,000. He also snapped up Jacob Littlejohn’s Over the Rills, the Crags, and the Hills (2025) from Karma gallery for $8,000.

Alain Servais, a Belgian collector, said he bought Ella Fleck’s Training Material (2026, one of three editions) from LA’s Ehrlich Steinberg gallery for £14,000 ($18,500).

By 3 p.m., Pace Gallery had sold most of its paintings by Brazilian artist Marina Perez Simão, valued at prices up to $250,000. Pace chief executive Marc Glimcher stressed to ARTnews the wide age range of collectors. “We had a lot of older collectors buy works today, someone in their 70s and a very young collector in their 20s,” he said.

Next door, Thaddaeus Ropac also nearly sold out, with work by Italian sculptor Leoncillo Leonardi (1915–68) drawing international buyers. Long revered by Italian connoisseurs but little known elsewhere, Leoncillo is enjoying something of a revival. Ropac announced representation in June, alongside the launch of a new foundation. The gallery’s top prices included Martha Jungwirth’s 202 painting Untitled (Berggasse 19) at €560,000, Antony Gormley’s Aside (2025) at £500,000, and Adrian Ghenie’s Untitled (2026) at €380,000.

Xavier Hufkens reported selling more than 16 pieces, including a work on paper by Richard Serra for $750,000, a suite of Louise Bourgeois works on paper for $400,000, and two neon works by Tracey Emin for prices between £95,000 and £105,000.

Several young galleries in the Focus section also did well. The Amsterdam-based Diez Gallery sold Jessica Wilson’s video installation Sweet Nothing(2025–26) for more than €20,000 to the Centraal Museum in Utrecht. “Last Frieze London for me was a very bad one, and since then, the gallery has been doing its best year in terms of finances and new collections,” dealer Diego Diez told ARTnews.

Dealer Gabriella Price from Heidi gallery told ARTnews that the business relocated from Berlin to London this year to “pursue fresh opportunities.” “London feels like a really fantastic city at this time, and the Focus section of Frieze gets so much attention with all the prize giving and funds that take place,” she said.

Dealer Adam D. Miller, of the Los Angeles–based gallery The Pit, returned to Frieze with renewed energy. He sold two thirds of the paintings from his solo booth for Bella Foster. “We want to develop more, particularly with European and UK institutions,” he told ARTnews.

Over at Frieze Masters, Andrew Edlin had a booth featuring the works of Frank Walter and Beverly Buchanan, whose work is in the Venice Biennale. The gallery said that a major museum board president—one that it did not name—purchased a 1990s work by Buchanan for a price between $65,000 and $125,000.

Robilant sold a mirror work by Michelangelo Pistoletto for €45,000 ($59,300) and two ceramics by Lucio Fontana, Bullfight for €125,000 ($164,900) and Concetto Spaziale for €250,000 ($329,700). “We have all seen the renewed interest in Old Masters as the pendulum swings from speculative to secure, and as clients look to artists who have already shown they can hold their value,” gallery director Michele di Robilant told ARTnews. He expressed optimism for the top of the market: “Clients are certainly finding their feet again at the top end. There is light at the end of the tunnel.”

item.title: Welcome to the ‘Uncanny Valley,’ the Haas Brothers’ Fantastic and Cheeky Universe - Colossal
item.description:
The imaginative, strange childhood dreams of twins Nikolai and Simon Haas materialize in a large-scale exhibition at Blanton Museum of Art. Working as the Haas Brothers, the siblings have been collaborating since 2010 and are widely known for their fantastical sculptures of flora and fauna with their signature cheeky, surreal twist. In Austin, the Los Angeles artists present a range of figurative furniture, plush cartoonish characters, and illuminated installations that showcase their idiosyncratic aesthetic.

Previously on view at Cranbrook Art Museum and the Museum of Art and Design in New York, Uncanny Valley is the first mid-career survey for the duo, presenting a range of their quirky, genre-defying works. The exhibition also nods to the brothers’ childhood in Austin, where they lived from age 3 to 19, a time when the unofficial city slogan “Keep Austin Weird” became a cultural ethos and early influence.

Interested in technology and its implications, the artists frequently engage with the strange intersection of the artificial and the natural. The duo’s brilliant and bizarre strawberry tree, for example, appears as if transplanted from another planet into the gallery. In a statement for the show, Simon elaborates:

The ‘uncanny valley’ generally refers to robotics, where empathy for a robot increases the more human you make it—up to a point. When the robot becomes too human, empathy switches to revulsion. The solution for this is to add cuteness: when a robot is humanoid with an extra dose of cuteness, empathy for the object skyrockets. Looking at our 15-year career from a bird’s-eye view, the ‘uncanny valley’ came into focus as a core theme.

Uncanny Valley is on view in Austin through January 17, when it will travel to its final location, Mint Museum in Charlotte. Find the accompanying monograph of the same name on Bookshop.

item.title: Who’s the Thief in Deana Lawson’s Photography? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
For her latest show, Deana Lawson made one simple request: no photography allowed. I watched as other gallery-goers entered and received the same mandate, while an attendant handed out Gagosian-branded stickers to cover phone cameras. I found myself watching the crowd, observing micro-expressions of discomfort and surprise. 

I imagine the rule against photography in our highly visual, largely immediate world can be unsettling, but is our attachment really that strong? In a society where most of us carry the vehicle of modern technological warfare in our pockets, Lawson’s prohibition on photography is certainly a sensible request. As I looked at the sticker plastered over my own camera, I felt that perhaps that sense of unmooring is precisely Lawson’s point.

Because I couldn’t take photos, as I thought about how to compose my thoughts for this piece, I found myself questioning my sight. This led me to then question my memory, my ability to hold onto the details that my phone usually carries. By the time I left, I wondered: Would I be able to recall the faces, the snapshots on display? Should I? In deference to Lawson’s vision, would I have to relinquish any desire writhing within me for a sense of control through these photographic constraints?

In Edge Control, an ongoing series that began in 2023, Lawson turns her attention to the ubiquity of everyday monitoring as it appears in the genre of the beauty-supply surveillance photo. These photos are typically pinned behind counters to deter theft, a long-held ritual of humiliation. In a recent interview, Lawson said of this work, “If anything, I feel more identity with the people on the wall — like I’m stealing a picture of them stealing.”

Yet by restricting access to what has become, for many, our second set of eyes, Lawson’s newest series provokes a fraught ethical question: Who truly has the power to authorize or deny access?

item.title: At Frieze, an Artist Project in the Fair’s Public Toilets Confronts the UK’s Ongoing Bathroom Wars - ARTnews.com
item.description:
At Frieze London this week, even the bathroom will be a place to see art. Gray Wielebinski’s new site-specific Production (2026) will transform the fair’s public toilets into an intimate olfactory environment, where scent, bodily function, privacy, desire, and surveillance will converge.

Rather than disappearing into the functional infrastructure of the bathroom, Production announces itself as an artwork: Custom urinal cakes and toilet-rim blocks infused with two scents are housed in sculptural cages, with security tags attached. They are strange, brightly colored, and scented. One is almost lipstick-red, while the other is black. Their texture is also different from typical urinal cakes. “They almost look like cosmetics, or like an art material,” he told ARTnews in an interview ahead of the work’s installation at the Regent’s Park.

The last time Frieze commissioned an artist to make work about its bathrooms was a decade ago, with Julie Verhoeven’s The Toilet Attendant… Now Wash Your Hands (2016), featuring the artist as the attendant in a piece of performance art. Like with Production, that work with its commentary on the ethics of labor in the art world, had a political dimension to it.

Made in collaboration with perfumier Dean’s Bottom, each of Production’s individual parts carries Wielebinski’s name and a security tag, and though they are not for sale, they are, technically, editioned. “It’s bringing up questions of value too,” he said, connecting it to the work’s overall setting, an art fair.

The objects’ sculptural cages add another layer to the work, connecting them to ideas of protection and exclusion. For Wielebinski, the bathroom is a particularly charged site, where the politics of gendered space have been used to police their use by transgender and gender non-conforming people.

Across the UK, new official guidance that came into force this past August states that single-sex spaces open to the public, including toilets and changing rooms in places like restaurants, gyms, hospital wards, and refuges, should be organized based on biological sex. The guidance, published by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), adds that trans people should use either gender-neutral facilities or the ones that match their biological sex. It comes after the UK Supreme Court ruled, in April 2025, that “sex” in equality law means “biological sex” rather than the gender someone identifies as. Trans-rights activists have strongly opposed the code’s implementation, with Trans+ Solidarity Alliance calling the gudiance “unworkable.”

“I think it’s something that I’m obviously very—I don’t want to say ‘drawn to’ but it impacts my life on a daily basis,” he said. “The bathroom holds a very fraught and also sacred and fun and ambivalent place in my world, in my life, in my psyche.”

Wielebinski first became interested in using scent for his 2023 installation Exhibition for the British department store Selfridges. “It started extremely organically,” Wielebinski said, describing his current olfactory obsession as a means of creating atmosphere and a way of translating between different mediums.

The scent of Production is also intentionally familiar, especially for any artists attending Frieze. Wielebinski describes them as “a take on the industrial smelling urinal cake that already exists that we’re used to smelling in the bathroom coinciding with a more conceptual scent based off of the scents of my studio.”

Wielebinski said he wasn’t quite sure what emotion Production will elicit of those who interact with it, though he expects a “wide range of feelings,” from attraction to disgust, curiosity to ambivalence. His intention isn’t one of provocation but to provide a collective experience to an otherwise private moment, or “a hushed secret thing that then also becomes communal in whatever way that might be,” he said, adding that he hopes it become the topic of conversations, jokes, and even criticism.

“Whenever you put work out in the world, it’s out of your hands, but I also think that’s, for me, when my work comes alive, when an audience interacts with it,” he said, noting that he wants to “draw people’s attention to all these things about what a bathroom can mean, and what a body can mean.”

item.title: ‘Radiant Geometries’ Illuminates Teachings and Technologies in the Indigenous Americas - Colossal
item.description:
For centuries, Navajo/Diné weavers have created intricate, geometrically patterned blankets and rugs on upright looms, powered only by the artisans’ bodies. More than a millennia ago in Mesoamerica, which encompassed much of what today is Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula and parts of Central America, the Mayans produced ornate ceramics decorated with natural motifs like birds. Utilizing materials that could be foraged or cultivated in the landscape—the Diné have herded the distinctive Navajo-Churro sheep since the breed was introduced by Spaniards in the 16th century—the techniques, motifs, and cultural customs continue to influence artists today.

Through the lens of Indigenous interpretations of mathematics, science, and architecture, Radiant Geometries: Vectors of Knowledge from the Indigenous Americas at Moody Center for the Arts at Rice University invites us into a multi-media encounter with a wide range of cosmological perspectives and views on nature, narrative, and innovation.

Curated by Noor Alé, the exhibition’s scope embraces South, Central, and North America as a whole to explore how contemporary Indigenous artists channel ancestral and technological knowledge. A wide range of paintings, sculpture, video, sound, and more delve into realms of the mathematical, metaphysical, social, and environmental, tapping into the artists’ distinctive backgrounds and cultural heritage.

Melissa Cody, for example, begins with a foundation in Diné weaving, drawing upon the teachings of three generations of makers before her. The artist utilizes both a vertical Navajo loom and a mechanized Jaquard machine to create vibrant textiles merging traditional motifs and patterns with contemporary designs and messages.

Eamon Ore-Giron’s large-scale geometric abstractions are a dominant force in Radiant Geometries, nodding to a range of Indigenous motifs and symbols, such as Native American medicine wheels and tapestries from the Amazon Basin. Influence also arises from the 20th-century pictorial language of geometric abstraction, especially hard-edge painting.

In the gallery, Ore-Giron’s works are foregrounded by a series of vivid, freestanding sculptures by Natalia Montoya Lecaros titled Tótems de emergencia. She pulls a figurative aesthetic thread from the garments of the Aymara people of the Andes, who are known for their vibrant, handcrafted clothing combining Indigenous clothing traditions with elements introduced by Spanish colonizers. In Tótems de emergencia, four upright, mixed-media pieces stand on “feet,” installed in a circle as if performing a ceremonial dance or tribute in the center of the gallery.

Additional artists featured in the exhibition include Patricia Domínguez, Jordan Ann Craig, Nanibah Chacon, Patrick Martinez, and many others. “At its core, Radiant Geometries centers Indigenous ways of knowing that continueto shape relationships to territories, waterways, and interspecies care,” Alé says.

The show runs through December 19 in Houston. The museum is also hosting a large-scale vinyl installation by Sharmistha Ray, which opens on October 22 and will remain on view through January 29. Explore all exhibitions on the Moody Center’s website.

item.title: Red Hook Open Studios Rises From the Ashes - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Red Hook’s arts community is nothing if not defiant in the face of tragedy. 

Nearly 13 months after a five-alarm fire scorched part of a historic Van Brunt Street warehouse, the Brooklyn waterfront neighborhood's open studios festival returned for its 11th year on October 10 and 11.

Some artists displaced by the fire have come back to the area too, moving into studios in nearby buildings closer to the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway. But the Civil War-era structure remained under a partial vacate order, with an unsightly green sidewalk shed surrounding part of the block just before the pier.

When festival co-coordinator Deborah Ugoretz distributed flyers promoting the event a few weeks ago, some residents told her they were surprised it was still happening. 

“They assumed that all the artists and makers in Red Hook were affected by the fire, but there are still hundreds of makers and artists here,” Ugoretz, whose studio a few doors down avoided fire and water damage, told Hyperallergic.

item.title: Congressional Commission to Consider Adding Jewish Museum to Smithsonian Network - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Weitzman National Museum of American Jewish History in Philadelphia is being considered as a potential new member of the Smithsonian museum network, with members of a new congressional commission sworn in on Tuesday set to study the matter.

As reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, Philip Darivoff, a former longtime chair of the Weitzman and current chair of the new commission, and Dara Horn, a writer serving as vice chair, “said that the Weitzman joining the Smithsonian would send a powerful message that Jews are a crucial component of the history of the country.”

Darivoff told the JTA, “It’s a different statement that our country makes when it says that the study of Jewish American history and culture is important to this nation,” and both commission members hope possible inclusion in the Smithsonian network could help stem what they called an “epidemic of ignorance” about Jewish history and culture.

The prospect of the Weitzman joining the Smithsonian dates back to legislation passed by the Biden administration in 2024 to establish the congressional commission. Now, after having been sworn in, the commission has two years to study the matter—“though Darivoff said he hopes to finish the work well before the deadline,” according to the JTA.

The Weitzman National Museum of American Jewish History was founded in 1976 and is currently a Smithsonian affiliate, which means it can share resources with other museums in the network. Current offerings there include a new “immersive family experience” called Colors of Creation, an exhibition titled “The First Salute: An Untold Story of the American Revolution,” and a core exhibition covering history dating back to the 1600s, “when the first permanent Jewish settlers came to the New World from Brazil.”

item.title: Richard Dadd’s Strange and Delicate Worlds - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LONDON — Most British viewers know Richard Dadd from “The Fairy Feller’s Master-Stroke,” replete with its controlled chaos of subject matter and unavoidable depiction of a man suffering from mental illness. The diminutively scaled work, now in Tate Britain’s permanent collection and on view at the Royal Academy of Art’s retrospective exhibition, Richard Dadd: Beyond Bedlam, was painted between 1855 and 1864 and worked over repeatedly for nearly a decade while Dadd was incarcerated at Bethlem Royal Hospital. The work is filled with minutely detailed fantastical figures and fairies, overlaid ad infinitum under a web of flowers and grass blades that bisect its surface. 

Dadd was born in 1817 in Chatham, England, worked during the Victorian era, and studied at the Royal Academy art schools. He was recognized as a leading talent among a group called The Clique, alongside other English artists such as Augustus Egg and William Powell Frith. But his biography is overshadowed by mental illness, which first became acutely evident on an expedition through Europe to Greece, Turkey, and Syria as a draftsman and culminated in a delusional episode in 1843 when he killed his own father and fled to France. After his arrest and return to England, authorities committed him to Bethlem Hospital's criminal department. 

Though his meticulously realized, highly individualized output sits largely outside the historical canon, the Royal Academy wisely avoids treating their new comprehensive survey of Dadd’s career as outsider art. The exhibition also avoids psychological interpretation and refers visitors to the Bethlem Museum of the Mind, from which many pieces have been loaned, for further medical and historical detail about Dadd’s stay there.

item.title: Ann Toebbe’s Skewed Paintings Transform Architectural Spaces into Cherished Places - Colossal
item.description:
“I find that when I work from my emotions and experiences, I make a more powerful image,” Ann Toebbe writes. Meditating on the connection between physical spaces and the feelings and memories bound within them is central to the Chicago artist’s practice.

In a review of Toebbe’s recent exhibition at Hyde Park Art Center, the writer Elisa Shoenberger teases out the distinction that grounds the artist’s work. “Space is the physical location, while place is the meaning we bring to it. It’s the difference between thinking about the physical location of your house (space) and the feelings, history and emotions tied up in your home (place),” Schoenberger writes. Rendering interiors and cross-cut buildings in impeccable detail, Toebbe concentrates on a particular sensation or mood and then constructs a series of architectural compositions that extrapolate on the theme.

Preliminary sketches and more elaborate drawings scaffold what becomes the final work on panel, which typically incorporates a mix of gouache, oil paint, paper collage, and colored pencil. Reference photos have their role, too, although each piece emerges with a manipulated layout and the artist’s signature skewed perspectives.

“I might extend a wall or include indoor and outdoor elements to make a layout snap together. I am always messing with how baseboards can divide and connect walls and floors. I might stack a composition or unfold it like a flattened box,” she says. “I love creating transitions with flow, and I try to avoid abrupt cropping.”

Toebbe’s stylized interiors typically mix reverse and parallel perspective, the former enlarging objects as they move farther away and the latter keeping objects the same size. This inventive approach plunges the viewer into an uncanny world in which the artist’s predilection toward pattern and texture reigns. “I like to change up working methods to give myself a new formal puzzle to solve,” she adds. “I usually have an idea of the materials I want to work with at the start, but everything is up for grabs as I work.”

If you’re in Chicago, you can see some of Toebbe’s works in a group exhibition on view through October 31 at Andrew Rafacz. Otherwise, find more from the artist on Instagram.

item.title: Art Problems: Do I Need an Agent? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
My career has stalled, and I spend more time on studio admin than actually working in it. I keep hearing about artist agents. I also keep hearing about AI agents that can do a lot of the administration for you. Do I need an agent or an agent? —Double Agent

I don’t know how much time you spend in the studio versus doing studio administration, but it sounds like the balance is off. The average artist should spend about 30 to 50% of their time on studio administration, depending on how they participate in the industry. And by studio administration, I mean the nuts-and-bolts stuff: inventory management, grant and residency applications, website maintenance. There are exceptions, and most artists will have stretches where admin takes over and vice versa. That’s normal. But the majority of your time shouldn’t be spent on administration. So, let’s get to fixing that.

First order of business: Artist agents are not the panacea we imagine them to be, assuming we can even agree on what they do. The term covers everything from estate planning to brand deals to career strategy. Few of them will write your applications or keep your inventory up to date. Fewer still place artists with galleries. Those agents are a bit like the narwhal, whose tusks were sold as unicorn horns in medieval Europe; the real thing exists, but it rarely lives up to the legend. It may be a spouse who runs the studio, or in one case I know of, a former gallerist placing artists who didn’t speak English at blue-chip galleries. The gallerist took 20% of sales, half from the artist and half from the gallery. It’s an expensive arrangement and it depended on the artists already having a market.

You keep hearing about these roles, though, because the market has had a few rough years. Sales by contemporary art dealers were stagnant in 2025, according to the Art Basel UBS Art Market Report. “Galleries are having to make thoughtful decisions about how they allocate their resources, and many can't carry the staff they once did,” consultant Kristen Becker of KB Art Strategies told me in a recent conversation. Becker offers strategic advice to galleries, nonprofits, artists, and art sponsors. “That means they can't always offer artists the level of support they used to, so we're seeing a range of services, including artist agents, step in to fill that gap.”

item.title: John Berger in His Own Bruised Time - Hyperallergic
item.description:
These days, we tend to take his ideas for granted: that art — making it or contemplating it — creates knowledge. That by foregrounding the processes by which we see, we can discover the mechanisms and deceptions through which we make meaning. And, of course, that it’s important to know who is footing the bill. John Berger, who died in 2017, was famous not for challenging the Western canon but for making its revelations feel so evidently connected to everything else about life. His essays often read like personal letters, offering to us the gift of our own passions and imaginations.

Berger was an electric presence in the 1972 BBC series Ways of Seeing, in which he appears to be standing in a museum, a kind of anarchist-angel with his unruly curls and groovy white shirt, slicing a detail out of a Botticelli with a box-cutter. This is revealed to be an illusion: The “museum” is in fact a television studio set, and the Botticelli is a reproduction. Berger was making a point about how technology changed the way we interact with images, but the subtext is clear: that he was there to cut through exclusionary and pedantic framings that, even a half-century later, persist in giving art a cordoned-off quality. 

A new biography, Tom Overton’s John Berger: From Life (2026), is less interested in applying the critic and Booker Prize-winning novelist’s ideas to our cultural moment, in which human creativity is vampirically extracted and homogenized by artificial intelligence, than it is in fixing him within his own bruised 20th century, shaped by modernization and imperialism. Overton and Berger met in 2009, when he donated his archive to the British Library; Overton edited two collections of Berger’s writing on art (Portraits: John Berger on Artists and Landscapes: John Berger on Art) and co-edited a collection of his essays on miners, The Underground Sea. Berger, whom Overton refers to as “John” throughout, granted the author permission to write his biography after his death. 

The result is deeply informative, deferential, and perceptive, sometimes lyrically so. In laying his thematic groundwork, Overton tells two stories. One is about Berger’s father, who, in the aftermath of World War I, remained in France to supervise the identification and transfer of fallen soldiers’ remains, “trying to give order and meaning to death.” The other draws from Berger’s memories as a teenager during the Blitz. Each month, he and his girlfriend would walk through bombed-out London to the National Gallery, where a single masterpiece at a time was shown — a lesson in survival “by our wits and with the Old Masters,” as Berger put it.

item.title: Roy Lichtenstein Was All Style - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Roy Lichtenstein's hand-painted Ben-Day dots, among his other cheeky twists on mass-produced gestures, were once "satirical and ironic commentaries on American consumerism," reflects critic John Yau. But what can they do for us in 2026? That’s the inquiry at the heart of Yau’s review of the new Lichtenstein retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American Art, an exhibition that, he argues, fails to reckon with the Pop titan’s anachronism and stylistic limitations.

With just three weeks to go before the critical midterm elections in the United States, Congress hopeful Jonathan Nez, former president of the Navajo Nation, is hoping to turn a red district blue in Arizona. On the heels of Indigenous Peoples’ Day, I spoke to him about how his Diné upbringing influenced his political thinking and Trump’s threats to sacred Native sites. 

Our conversation comes right as advocacy groups sue the federal government to protect Utah’s Nine Mile Canyon from oil tanker truck transit that could threaten ancient petroglyphs — Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar has that story.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Jonathan Nez on Indigenous Perseverance

This November, Jonathan Nez could become the first Native American to represent Arizona in Congress. Nez, who served as president of the Navajo Nation from 2019 to 2023, is running to flip the state’s largest congressional district by area, a seat currently held by Republican Eli Crane. His “Warrior Up” platform is structured into four pillars, a tribute to the number’s significance to Diné people, for whom the world is bound by four sacred mountains, one in each cardinal direction. | Valentina Di Liscia
